CausalChain: HCC cells exhibit altered methionine metabolism -> Excess production of SAM and MTA occurs -> SAM/MTA mediate epigenetic modifications in nearby T cells -> Upregulation of exhaustion markers (e.g., PD-1, CTLA-4) in T lymphocytes -> Impaired cytotoxic function and T cell exhaustion -> Establishment of an immunosuppressive TME
Hypothesis: Modulating the methionine metabolism of HCC cells to reduce the excessive production of SAM and MTA will reverse the epigenetic reprogramming leading to T cell exhaustion, thereby restoring effective anti-tumor immune responses and enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapeutic strategies in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by a complex interplay between malignant cells and a diverse tumor microenvironment (TME). Among the multiple mechanisms contributing to tumor immune evasion, metabolic reprogramming in HCC cells has garnered increasing attention. In particular, altered methionine metabolism in HCC leads to excessive production of metabolites such as S‐adenosylmethionine (SAM) and methylthioadenosine (MTA), which have been implicated in inducing epigenetic modifications in immune cells. Here, we propose that heightened production of SAM/MTA by HCC cells drives chromatin remodeling in tumor‐infiltrating T lymphocytes, thereby upregulating exhaustion markers including PD‐1 and CTLA‐4. This metabolic‐epigenetic reprogramming contributes to T cell dysfunction and promotes an immunosuppressive microenvironment that supports tumor progression. Targeting the critical nodes in tumor methionine metabolism may therefore reverse T cell exhaustion and improve responses to immunotherapies.
